description_full: Archer-Daniels-Midland Company provides human and animal nutrition ingredients and solutions in the United States, Switzerland, the Cayman Islands, Brazil, Mexico, Canada, the United Kingdom, and internationally. It operates in three segments: Ag Services and Oilseeds; Carbohydrate Solutions; and Nutrition. The company engages in the origination, merchandising, transportation, and storage of agricultural raw materials, as well as the crushing and processing of oilseeds, including soybeans and soft seeds, such as cottonseed, sunflower seed, canola, rapeseed, and flaxseed; produces and markets vegetable oils and oilseed protein meals used by food, feed, energy, and industrial customers; sale of crude and partially refined vegetable oils; supplies peanuts and peanut-derived ingredients; and manufactures cotton cellulose pulp. It is also involved in the grain sourcing, handling, and multimodal transportation network supporting import, export, and distribution activities; structured trade finance activities; corn and wheat wet and dry milling and related processing activities; production of distillers' grains, corn gluten feed, and corn gluten meal for use as animal feed ingredients; and carbon capture and sequestration and other emissions-reduction initiatives. In addition, the company engages in the creation, manufacturing, sale, and distribution of an array of ingredients and solutions comprising plant-based proteins, flavors and colors derived from nature, flavor systems, emulsifiers, soluble fiber, polyols, hydrocolloids, probiotics, prebiotics, postbiotics, enzymes, botanical extracts, and other specialty food and feed ingredients and systems. Further, it is involved in the derivatives and commodity exchanges and clearing houses; and insurance coverage for certain property, casualty, marine, medical, and other miscellaneous risks. The company was founded in 1902 and is based in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Archer-Daniels-Midland Company is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $34.7B market cap on $80.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 10% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 6% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $4.2B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.06× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 3.1×.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sect: Its 2% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.29x its revenue share).
It accounts for 2.4% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 46% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.55, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.29 vs 5y 0.43), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $257.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 27% in the 2022 bear market and 68% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 47% below its DCF fair value of $138, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 34%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $99.01 to $197 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 14.2 vs 18.3 and P/FCF 8.3 vs 16.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 136% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 12.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $78.50 on average, 8% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 7.2%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.32).
It runs a 6% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.1% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.4x net debt to EBITDA ($1.0B of cash against $8.4B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 3.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.5% over 3 years, 4.5% over 5 years and 1.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 1.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 10, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 13.9% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase, net $197K bought).
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (2.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 42 consecutive years, raising it 4.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 40,798 employees, each generates about $2.0M of revenue, 3.9x the Consumer Defensive median.
That works out to $103K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.1M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
